{{Short description|Test for the acceptability of conditionals via hypothetical belief revision}}
{{about|the test for conditionals|a branch of combinatorics named after Frank P. Ramsey|Ramsey theory}}
{{AI-generated|reason=see the explanation at [[Special:PermanentLink/1368212033#Query]]|date=August 2026}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2025}}

The '''Ramsey test''' (also called the '''Ramsey test for conditionals''') is a proposal for how to evaluate and accept conditional sentences of the form ''if'' ''p'' ''(then)'' ''q''. Informally, the guiding idea is that, to decide whether to accept a conditional if-p-then-q in a given belief state ''K'', one must hypothetically add ''p'' to ''K'' and revise ''K'' in a minimal and rational way to accommodate ''p''; then, one must accept if-p-then-q if, and only if, q would be accepted in the resulting belief state.<ref name="Ramsey1929">{{cite book |last=Ramsey |first=Frank P. |author-link=Frank P. Ramsey |year=1929 |title=The Foundations of Mathematics and Other Logical Essays |editor-last=Braithwaite |editor-first=R. B. |publisher=Routledge & Kegan Paul |chapter=General Propositions and Causality |pages=237–255}}</ref><ref name="SEP-Ramsey">{{cite encyclopedia |last=MacBride |first=Fraser |year=2019 |title=Frank Ramsey |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ramsey/}}</ref> In contemporary formulations, the "minimal" change of belief is made precise by a belief revision operation or by a rule for changing probabilities or possible-world rankings, depending on the framework.<ref name="Gardenfors1986" /><ref name="BradleyDefence">{{cite journal |last=Bradley |first=Richard |year=2001 |title=A Defence of the Ramsey Test |journal=Mind |volume=110 |issue=439 |pages=689–712 |doi=10.1093/mind/110.439.689}}</ref><ref name="Guenther2022" />

The test originates in a brief footnote in [[Frank P. Ramsey]]'s 1929 essay ''General Propositions and Causality'', but has since been developed in several overlapping research traditions, namely, in the theory of {{section link||Belief revision}}, in {{section link||Probabilistic approaches to conditionals}}, in {{section link||Possible-worlds semantics}}, and in dynamic and non-monotonic logics.<ref name="Guenther2022">{{cite journal |last=Günther |first=Mario |year=2022 |title=Ramsey's conditionals |journal=Synthese |volume=200 |issue=5 |pages=1–34 |article-number=165 |doi=10.1007/s11229-022-03586-1}}</ref><ref name="SEP-LogicCond">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Egré |first=Paul |year=2021 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-conditionals/}}</ref> The Ramsey test has also been shown to generate various "triviality" results when combined with seemingly natural constraints on rational belief change, leading to an extensive literature on how it should be formulated and where its limits lie.<ref name="Gardenfors1986">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1986 |title=Belief Revisions and the Ramsey Test for Conditionals |journal=The Philosophical Review |volume=95 |issue=1 |pages=81–93 |doi=10.2307/2185133 |jstor=2185133}}</ref><ref name="Gardenfors1987">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1987 |title=Variations on the Ramsey test: More triviality results |journal=Synthese |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=69–85 |doi=10.1007/BF00485169 |doi-broken-date=7 January 2026 }}</ref><ref name="Leitgeb2010">{{cite journal |last=Leitgeb |first=Hannes |year=2010 |title=On the Ramsey Test Without Triviality |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=21–54 |doi=10.1215/00294527-2010-003}}</ref>

== Historical background ==

=== Ramsey's footnote ===
Ramsey's discussion of conditionals appears in a single footnote to ''General Propositions and Causality'' (1929), posthumously published in ''The Foundations of Mathematics and Other Logical Essays'':<ref name="Ramsey19292">{{cite book |last=Ramsey |first=Frank P. |author-link=Frank P. Ramsey |title=The Foundations of Mathematics and Other Logical Essays |publisher=Routledge & Kegan Paul |year=1929 |editor-last=Braithwaite |editor-first=R. B. |pages=237–255 |chapter=General Propositions and Causality}}</ref><blockquote>If two people are arguing "If p will q?" and are both in doubt as to p, they are adding p hypothetically to their stock of knowledge and arguing on that basis about q; so that in a sense "If p, q" and "If p, ¬q" are contradictories. We can say they are fixing their degrees of belief in q given p. If p turns out false, these degrees of belief are rendered void. If either party believes ¬p for certain, the question ceases to mean anything to him except as a question about what follows from certain laws or hypotheses.<ref>{{cite book |last=Harper |first=William L. |chapter=A Sketch of Some Recent Developments in the Theory of Conditionals |date=1981  |pages=3–38 |editor-last=Harper |editor-first=William L. |title=IFS |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-9117-0_1 |access-date=2025-12-03 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-9117-0_1 |isbn=978-94-009-9117-0 |editor2-last=Stalnaker |editor2-first=Robert |editor3-last=Pearce |editor3-first=Glenn}}</ref></blockquote>Ramsey connects conditionals with what he calls "variable hypotheticals", general rules of the form "if anything is ''F'' it is ''G''", which, on his view, function as laws or policies guiding future judgement and action. To Ramsey, believing a conditional is adopting a rule such that, under the supposition of ''p'' together with one's background information and laws, one is disposed to accept ''q''.<ref name="SEP-Ramsey2">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2019 |title=Frank Ramsey |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ramsey/ |last=MacBride |first=Fraser |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref><ref name="Guenther20224">{{cite journal |last=Günther |first=Mario |year=2022 |title=Ramsey's conditionals |journal=Synthese |volume=200 |issue=5 |pages=1–34 |article-number=165 |doi=10.1007/s11229-022-03586-1}}</ref>

Although Ramsey's writings on conditionals attracted relatively little attention at first, the footnote was rediscovered in the later twentieth century, where it came to be seen as a key inspiration for non-material accounts of conditionals in [[philosophy of language]], epistemology, and formal logic.<ref name="SEP-LogicCond7">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2021 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-conditionals/ |last=Egré |first=Paul |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref><ref name="Guenther20223">{{cite journal |last=Günther |first=Mario |year=2022 |title=Ramsey's conditionals |journal=Synthese |volume=200 |issue=5 |pages=1–34 |article-number=165 |doi=10.1007/s11229-022-03586-1}}</ref>

=== Later developments ===
From the 1960s onwards, Ramsey's idea was taken up in at least three overlapping research programmes:

* In ''possible-worlds semantics'', philosophers Robert Stalnaker and David Lewis model the hypothetical addition of ''p'' by selecting a "closest" or most plausible ''p''-world to evaluate ''q'' at, which is an approach to conditionals inspired by the Ramsey test.<ref name="SEP-IndCond4">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2001 |title=Indicative Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/conditionals/ |last=Edgington |first=Dorothy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref>
* In ''probabilistic'' approaches, the Ramsey test is read as a recipe for tying the acceptability of conditionals to conditional probabilities.<ref name="SEP-IndCond4" /><ref name="SEP-LogicCond6">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2021 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-conditionals/ |last=Egré |first=Paul |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref>
* In ''belief revision theory'', especially the AGM framework, the Ramsey test is the inspiration for an equivalence between a belief set's acceptance of a conditional and the consequent's membership in belief set after it is revised by the antecedent.<ref name="Lindstrom19927">{{cite journal |last=Lindström |first=Sten |year=1992 |title=Belief revision, epistemic conditionals and the Ramsey test |journal=Synthese |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=343–358 |doi=10.1007/BF00413567}}</ref><ref name="Gardenfors19864">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1986 |title=Belief Revisions and the Ramsey Test for Conditionals |journal=The Philosophical Review |volume=95 |issue=1 |pages=81–93 |doi=10.2307/2185133 |jstor=2185133}}</ref>

Subsequent work has elaborated versions of the Ramsey test in dynamic epistemic logic, non-monotonic reasoning, game theory, and artificial intelligence, often under the heading of "epistemic" or "subjunctive" conditionals.<ref name="KernIsberner19994">{{cite conference |last=Kern-Isberner |first=Gabriele |year=1999 |title=Proceedings of the Sixteenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-99) |url=https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/99-1/Papers/028.pdf |pages=186–191 |chapter=Postulates for Conditional Belief Revision}}</ref><ref name="Rott20105">{{cite book |last=Rott |first=Hans |url=https://epub.uni-regensburg.de/26003/ |title=Conditionals, Probability and Paradox |publisher=College Publications |year=2011 |editor-last=Bernardi |editor-first=Claudio |pages=101–134 |chapter=Reapproaching Ramsey: Conditionals and Iterated Belief Change in the Spirit of AGM}}</ref> The precise formulations vary; Bradley argues that the Ramsey test should be seen as a [[Axiom schema|schema]] that can be instantiated in different ways for different kinds of conditionals and different models of belief change.<ref name="BradleyDefence2">{{cite journal |last=Bradley |first=Richard |year=2001 |title=A Defence of the Ramsey Test |url=https://personal.lse.ac.uk/bradleyr/pubs.html |journal=Mind |volume=110 |issue=439 |pages=689–712 |doi=10.1093/mind/110.439.689}}</ref>

== Formalizations ==

=== Belief revision ===
In AGM belief revision, a belief state is represented by a deductively closed set of sentences ''K'', and revision by a new sentence ''p'' is represented by an operator ''*'' that outputs a new belief set ''K* p''. The Ramsey test is then commonly expressed as a definitional equivalence for an epistemic conditional connective ''>'':

: '''Ramsey test (AGM form).'''
: ''K'' accepts the conditional ''p > q'' if and only if ''q'' is a member of the revised belief set ''K * p''. That is, <math>p > q \in K \quad\text{iff}\quad q \in K * p.</math>

This formulation connects a [[Conditional logic|logic of conditionals]] with a [[Belief revision|belief revision theory]], so that principles about the conditional connective ''>'' can be translated into postulates on the revision operation ''*'', and conversely.<ref name="Lindstrom19926">{{cite journal |last=Lindström |first=Sten |year=1992 |title=Belief revision, epistemic conditionals and the Ramsey test |journal=Synthese |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=343–358 |doi=10.1007/BF00413567}}</ref><ref name="Gardenfors19863">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1986 |title=Belief Revisions and the Ramsey Test for Conditionals |journal=The Philosophical Review |volume=95 |issue=1 |pages=81–93 |doi=10.2307/2185133 |jstor=2185133}}</ref>

=== Probabilistic approaches to conditionals ===
Some formulations read the Ramsey test as inherently probabilistic. On this view, to evaluate ''if p, q'' one should adjust one's credence function as if ''p'' were known and then look at the resulting probability of ''q''.

An influential proposal, called "the Ramsey–Adams thesis" or "Adams's thesis", holds that, for suitable indicative conditionals, the acceptability or assertability of ''if p, q'' is governed by the conditional probability <math>P(q \mid p)</math>.<ref name="SEP-IndCond3">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2001 |title=Indicative Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/conditionals/ |last=Edgington |first=Dorothy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref><ref name="SEP-LogicCond5">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2021 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-conditionals/ |last=Egré |first=Paul |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref> Some proposals, such as Robert Stalnaker's, go further and identify the ''probability of the conditional'' with the corresponding ''conditional probability'', e.g. <math>P(\text{if }p,q)=P(q\mid p)</math>.<ref name="Stalnaker19702">{{cite journal |last=Stalnaker |first=Robert C. |year=1970 |title=Probability and Conditionals |journal=Philosophy of Science |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=64–80 |doi=10.1086/288308}}</ref> However, in 1976, philosopher [[David Lewis (philosopher)|David Lewis]] proved a famous series of ''triviality results'' which show that, under plausible assumptions, such equations cannot hold generally for non-trivial probability functions, motivating weaker connections between conditional probability and conditional acceptability.<ref name="SEP-LogicCond4">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2021 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-conditionals/ |last=Egré |first=Paul |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref>

A related line of work studies how probabilities for compounds and embeddings of conditionals can be assigned while avoiding triviality, for example by restricting the language or weakening closure assumptions.<ref name="Leitgeb201022">{{cite journal |last=Leitgeb |first=Hannes |year=2010 |title=On the Ramsey Test Without Triviality |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=21–54 |doi=10.1215/00294527-2010-003}}</ref><ref name="McGee1989">{{cite journal |last=McGee |first=Vann |year=1989 |title=Conditional Probabilities and Compounds of Conditionals |journal=The Philosophical Review |volume=98 |issue=4 |pages=485–541 |doi=10.2307/2185116 |jstor=2185116}}</ref>

=== Possible-worlds semantics ===
In [[Conditional logic|conditional logics]] with possible-worlds semantics, the idea of a ''selection function'', introduced by [[Robert Stalnaker]], assigns to each world ''w'' and antecedent ''p'' a set of "closest" or most plausible ''p''-worlds, and the conditional "if p, q" is true at ''w'' when all of these selected worlds satisfy ''q''.<ref name="SEP-LogicCond3">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2021 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-conditionals/ |last=Egré |first=Paul |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref> Stalnaker explicitly claimed that the idea was inspired by the Ramsey test.<ref>{{cite book  |last=Harper |first=William L. |chapter=A Sketch of Some Recent Developments in the Theory of Conditionals |date=1981   |pages=3–38 |editor-last=Harper |editor-first=William L. |title=IFS |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-9117-0_1 |access-date=2025-12-03 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-9117-0_1 |isbn=978-94-009-9117-0 |editor2-last=Stalnaker |editor2-first=Robert |editor3-last=Pearce |editor3-first=Glenn}}</ref><ref name="Stalnaker19682">{{cite journal |last=Stalnaker |first=Robert C. |year=1968 |title=A Theory of Conditionals |journal=Studies in Logical Theory |pages=98–112}}</ref> Stalnaker assumed a unique closest world, while David Lewis weakened this to a set of closest worlds.<ref name="Lewis1973Comparative">{{cite journal |last=Lewis |first=David K. |year=1973 |title=Counterfactuals and Comparative Possibility |journal=Journal of Philosophical Logic |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=418–446 |doi=10.1007/BF00262950}}</ref>

== Triviality theorem in belief revision ==
When the AGM form of the Ramsey test is combined with the standard AGM postulates for rational belief revision, one obtains strong constraints on the interaction between conditionals and revision. Gärdenfors showed that combining (i) the Ramsey-test link between an epistemic conditional and revision, (ii) standard AGM postulates, and (iii) the assumption that conditionals can appear as ordinary beliefs and as inputs to revision, yields "triviality" or "impossibility" results: the only revision operators satisfying all constraints behave degenerately or collapse distinctions between belief states.<ref name="LindstromRabinowicz1992">{{cite journal |last1=Lindström |first1=Sten |last2=Rabinowicz |first2=Wlodzimierz |year=1992 |title=Belief Revision, Epistemic Conditionals and the Ramsey Test |journal=Synthese |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=195–237 |doi=10.1007/BF00413567}}</ref><ref name="Gardenfors19862">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1986 |title=Belief Revisions and the Ramsey Test for Conditionals |journal=The Philosophical Review |volume=95 |issue=1 |pages=81–93 |doi=10.2307/2185133 |jstor=2185133}}</ref>

In subsequent work, Gärdenfors proposed weakened versions of the test and explored further triviality theorems, including results for negative conditionals ("the negative Ramsey test").<ref name="Gardenfors19875">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1987 |title=Variations on the Ramsey test: More triviality results |journal=Synthese |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=69–85 |doi=10.1007/BF00485169 |doi-broken-date=7 January 2026 }}</ref>

=== Responses and modifications ===
A large literature investigates how to preserve the explanatory appeal of Ramsey testing while avoiding triviality. Prominent strategies include:

* Restricting the language so that conditionals are not themselves items that can be straightforwardly revised upon (or limiting which embeddings are allowed).<ref name="Lindstrom19925">{{cite journal |last=Lindström |first=Sten |year=1992 |title=Belief revision, epistemic conditionals and the Ramsey test |journal=Synthese |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=343–358 |doi=10.1007/BF00413567}}</ref>
* Weakening or modifying revision postulates (for example, weakening strong preservation/minimal-change requirements for conditionals).<ref name="LindstromRabinowicz19923">{{cite journal |last=Bradley |first=Richard |year=2001 |title=A Defence of the Ramsey Test |url=https://personal.lse.ac.uk/bradleyr/pubs.html |journal=Mind |volume=110 |issue=439 |pages=689–712 |doi=10.1093/mind/110.439.689}}</ref><ref name="Lindstrom19924">{{cite journal |last=Lindström |first=Sten |year=1992 |title=Belief revision, epistemic conditionals and the Ramsey test |journal=Synthese |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=343–358 |doi=10.1007/BF00413567}}</ref>
* Weakening the Ramsey test itself, such as by limiting it to certain classes of conditionals (for example, epistemic rather than metaphysical conditionals),<ref name="Leitgeb20105">{{cite journal |last=Leitgeb |first=Hannes |year=2010 |title=On the Ramsey Test Without Triviality |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=21–54 |doi=10.1215/00294527-2010-003}}</ref> or reinterpreting the test as an assertability norm rather than as defining truth conditions for a conditional proposition.
* Replacing belief sets with richer epistemic states, such as plausibility orderings or ranking functions, allowing more fine-grained "minimal change" dynamics compatible with the Ramsey test.<ref name="Gardenfors19873">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1987 |title=Variations on the Ramsey test: More triviality results |journal=Synthese |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=69–85 |doi=10.1007/BF00485169 |doi-broken-date=7 January 2026 }}</ref><ref name="Gardenfors19874">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1987 |title=Variations on the Ramsey test: More triviality results |journal=Synthese |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=69–85 |doi=10.1007/BF00485169 |doi-broken-date=7 January 2026 }}</ref><ref name="Leitgeb20104">{{cite journal |last=Leitgeb |first=Hannes |year=2010 |title=On the Ramsey Test Without Triviality |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=21–54 |doi=10.1215/00294527-2010-003}}</ref><ref name="Rott20104">{{cite book |last=Rott |first=Hans |url=https://epub.uni-regensburg.de/26003/ |title=Conditionals, Probability and Paradox |publisher=College Publications |year=2011 |editor-last=Bernardi |editor-first=Claudio |pages=101–134 |chapter=Reapproaching Ramsey: Conditionals and Iterated Belief Change in the Spirit of AGM}}</ref>

== Negative and iterated Ramsey tests ==
Besides the positive Ramsey test for accepting ''if p, q'', there are proposals for "negative Ramsey tests" that aim to characterise when a conditional of the form ''if p, not q'' should be rejected or accepted. These have been shown to generate further triviality results when combined with standard belief-revision postulates, prompting more fine-grained treatments of denial and of conditionals with negative consequents.<ref name="Gardenfors19872">{{cite journal |last=Gärdenfors |first=Peter |year=1987 |title=Variations on the Ramsey test: More triviality results |journal=Synthese |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=69–85 |doi=10.1007/BF00485169 |doi-broken-date=7 January 2026 }}</ref>

A further extension concerns ''iterated'' Ramsey tests, where conditionals are evaluated relative to sequences of revisions rather than single steps. This connects the Ramsey test with work on iterated belief revision and [[Dynamic epistemic logic|dynamic epistemic logics]], in which the evolution of an agent's plausibility ordering under multiple pieces of information is explicitly modelled.<ref name="Rott20103">{{cite book |last=Rott |first=Hans |url=https://epub.uni-regensburg.de/26003/ |title=Conditionals, Probability and Paradox |publisher=College Publications |year=2011 |editor-last=Bernardi |editor-first=Claudio |pages=101–134 |chapter=Reapproaching Ramsey: Conditionals and Iterated Belief Change in the Spirit of AGM}}</ref><ref name="KernIsberner19993">{{cite conference |last=Kern-Isberner |first=Gabriele |year=1999 |title=Proceedings of the Sixteenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-99) |url=https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/99-1/Papers/028.pdf |pages=186–191 |chapter=Postulates for Conditional Belief Revision}}</ref>

== Applications ==
The Ramsey test is a strategy to develop a semantics for conditionals. As such, it is part of the philosophy of language as well as the linguistic semantics of natural language.<ref name="SEP-LogicCond2">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2021 |title=The Logic of Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-conditionals/ |last=Egré |first=Paul |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref><ref name="SEP-IndCond2">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2001 |title=Indicative Conditionals |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/conditionals/ |last=Edgington |first=Dorothy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N.}}</ref> Due to the importance of hypothetical conditionals for reasoning, the Ramsey test is also applied in formal epistemology and belief revision (representation theorems and postulates governing rational change of view),<ref name="SEP-LogicCond2" /><ref name="Lindstrom19922">{{cite journal |last=Lindström |first=Sten |year=1992 |title=Belief revision, epistemic conditionals and the Ramsey test |journal=Synthese |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=343–358 |doi=10.1007/BF00413567}}</ref> artificial intelligence and non-monotonic belief management systems (defaults, conditional rules, and systems for reasoning under hypothetical assumptions),<ref name="KernIsberner19992">{{cite conference |last=Kern-Isberner |first=Gabriele |year=1999 |title=Proceedings of the Sixteenth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-99) |url=https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/99-1/Papers/028.pdf |pages=186–191 |chapter=Postulates for Conditional Belief Revision}}</ref><ref name="Rott20102">{{cite book |last=Rott |first=Hans |url=https://epub.uni-regensburg.de/26003/ |title=Conditionals, Probability and Paradox |publisher=College Publications |year=2011 |editor-last=Bernardi |editor-first=Claudio |pages=101–134 |chapter=Reapproaching Ramsey: Conditionals and Iterated Belief Change in the Spirit of AGM}}</ref> and dynamic logics of information (iterated revision and the semantics/pragmatics of conditional discourse).<ref name="Leitgeb20103">{{cite journal |last=Leitgeb |first=Hannes |year=2010 |title=On the Ramsey Test Without Triviality |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=21–54 |doi=10.1215/00294527-2010-003}}</ref> It plays a role in many current approaches to modelling learning, decision-making under uncertainty, and the social aggregation of conditional opinions.<ref name="Leitgeb20102">{{cite journal |last=Leitgeb |first=Hannes |year=2010 |title=On the Ramsey Test Without Triviality |journal=Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=21–54 |doi=10.1215/00294527-2010-003}}</ref><ref name="Guenther20222">{{cite journal |last=Günther |first=Mario |year=2022 |title=Ramsey's conditionals |journal=Synthese |volume=200 |issue=5 |pages=1–34 |article-number=165 |doi=10.1007/s11229-022-03586-1}}</ref>
